title: Wall Street Edges Higher as Earnings Beat Expectations Despite Middle East Tensions
excerpt: US stocks posted modest gains on Friday as strong corporate results from technology and consumer companies outweighed persistent geopolitical concerns, with the S&P 500 rising for the first time in three sessions.
body:
• US stocks posted modest gains on Friday, with the S&P 500 rising for the first time in three sessions as strong corporate earnings outweighed geopolitical concerns.
  • Technology and consumer companies reported better-than-expected quarterly results, providing a floor for equities despite elevated oil prices.
  • Investors are closely watching tariff policy developments, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signaling a possible tariff deal with the EU could be reached before August.
  • The divergence between rising US markets and falling Indian markets highlights how the Middle East crisis is hitting emerging economies harder than developed ones.

US stocks edged higher on Friday as investors weighed a batch of better-than-expected corporate earnings against persistent risks from the Middle East conflict and ongoing tariff uncertainty, ending a choppy week on a cautiously optimistic note.

The S&P 500 rose for the first time in three sessions, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average and Nasdaq Composite also posted modest gains. The recovery came after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signaled that a tariff deal with the European Union could be reached before August, easing one of the market's key concerns.

Earnings Provide a Floor

Strong quarterly results from several large-cap companies helped support sentiment. Technology firms and consumer-facing companies reported revenue and profit numbers that exceeded analyst expectations, suggesting the US economy remains resilient despite elevated interest rates and trade policy uncertainty.

The earnings season has been broadly encouraging, with roughly 78% of S&P 500 companies that have reported so far beating consensus estimates — slightly above the long-term average. However, forward guidance has been cautious, with many executives flagging the potential impact of tariffs and energy costs on second-half margins.

Geopolitical Risks Persist

The gains were tempered by continued uncertainty around the US-Iran conflict. Brent crude remained above $100 per barrel following this week's Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, though prices stabilized on Friday after several volatile sessions.

Defense and energy stocks outperformed, while airlines and transportation companies lagged as investors priced in higher fuel costs. The VIX volatility index edged lower but remained elevated compared to its levels before the conflict escalated.

Two Markets, Two Stories

For NRI investors with portfolios spanning both US and Indian markets, the week highlighted a stark divergence. While Wall Street managed gains on the back of strong domestic earnings, Indian markets suffered their worst five-day stretch in years as the oil price spike disproportionately hit Asia's crude-importing economies.

The Sensex fell roughly 3% for the week while the S&P 500 ended modestly higher — a reminder that geopolitical shocks can affect developed and emerging markets very differently, even when the underlying event is the same.

Next week, investors will be watching for more earnings reports from mega-cap technology companies, further developments in Middle East diplomacy, and any concrete progress on tariff negotiations with the EU and other trading partners.
nri_angle: NRI investors with US market exposure are navigating a complex landscape where strong corporate earnings compete with Middle East-driven oil price shocks hitting Indian markets.
